title: Drift or Selection? Chance in Small Populations
subject: biology
goal: Find out how chance alone changes a small population's genes from one generation to the next, and how that differs from natural selection.
steps: Split into two pairs. Each pair has a population of 10 gene copies: put 5 A and 5 a tokens in your cup. Record generation 0.
Pair 1 is drift only. Pair 2 adds selection: each time you draw an a, roll the die; on 1 or 2 that copy doesn't survive, so put it back and draw again.
Make the next generation: draw one token without looking, write down its letter, and put it back. Do this 10 times.
Set your cup to match: as many A tokens as you drew A's, and a tokens for the rest. Record the number of A.
Repeat for up to 12 generations, or until a cup is all A or all a. Then compare the two pairs.

table.title: Number of A copies in each cup

listen_for: Surprise when the drift cup loses A with nothing favoring a. Ask: what was different about a, if anything?
Draws that aren't blind or aren't put back. The Skeptic watches the draws.
“Selection always wins.” Ask what happened in other groups' selection cups.
debrief: Tally the class: how many drift cups ended all A, all a, or mixed? How many selection cups? Ask what the difference shows.
Ask: why do endangered species with tiny populations lose genetic variety even when nothing is selecting against it?
sources: The idea is also modeled in NetLogo's GenDrift models (Wilensky, Northwestern University) and HHMI BioInteractive's population genetics tools. The activity and questions were written for Paper Loop.
